title: How the internet works end to end
scopeHtml: Scope: what happens when you type a URL, OSI vs TCP/IP layers, packets and frames.

notes.title: What a network is
notes.html:
A network is machines that agree on rules (protocols) for sending bits to each other. Your phone, a router, a server in Mumbai: all just computers that pass small chunks of data and follow shared rules so everyone understands them.

The internet is not one network. It is about 100,000+ independent networks (called autonomous systems: ISPs, clouds, universities, companies) glued together by agreements. No one owns it. That is why "the internet" keeps working even when parts break.

Worked example. A page of 2 MB is not sent as one blob. At about 1,460 bytes of payload per packet it becomes about 1,440 packets, each routed independently and put back in order at the other end.

Industry examples. Google runs its own private global backbone (B4 and others) so traffic between its data centers does not touch the public internet. Cloudflare and Netflix put servers inside ISPs (Netflix Open Connect) to shorten the path.

Everyday analogy. The postal system: no single owner, many local post offices, each follows the same address format and hands letters to the next office.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the internet is a cloud". It is physical cables (about 95% of intercontinental traffic goes via undersea fibre).
  • Treating the internet as reliable. It is best effort; packets are lost, reordered and duplicated, and higher layers fix that.

notes.title: Packets, frames and encapsulation
notes.html:
Data is cut into small pieces, and each piece gets a header (an envelope) added by every layer on the way down. This wrapping is called encapsulation.

  • Segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP): adds ports.
  • Packet: adds source and destination IP address.
  • Frame: adds source and destination MAC address, for one hop on one link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi).

At each router the frame is thrown away and rebuilt for the next link; the packet inside stays (the TTL goes down by 1).

HTTP data      "GET / HTTP/1.1 ..."                       (say 500 bytes)
+ TCP header   20 B   src port 51234, dst port 443        -> segment 520 B
+ IP header    20 B   src 192.168.1.5, dst 142.250.x.x    -> packet  540 B
+ Ethernet     14 B header + 4 B CRC trailer              -> frame   558 B
(on the wire also: 8 B preamble + 12 B inter-frame gap)

Worked example (overhead). Sending 1 byte of data over TCP/IPv4/Ethernet costs 1 + 20 + 20 + 18 = 59 bytes, and the Ethernet minimum frame is 64 bytes, so padding is added. Tiny messages are mostly header. A full 1,500-byte MTU packet is 1,460 B payload out of about 1,538 on the wire, roughly 95% efficient.

Industry examples. High-frequency trading firms care about every header byte. Games send small UDP packets (20 to 100 bytes) and accept the overhead. Wireshark and tcpdump show exactly these layers.

Everyday analogy. A gift in a box (data), inside a courier bag with the city address (IP), inside a truck crate labelled for the next depot (frame). Each depot re-crates it.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up frame (link layer, MAC) and packet (network layer, IP).
  • Forgetting MTU: 1,500 B is the typical Ethernet payload limit, not the frame size.

notes.title: OSI vs TCP/IP layers
notes.html:
OSI is a 7-layer teaching model; TCP/IP is the 4 or 5-layer model the real internet uses. Interviewers use OSI numbers as vocabulary ("L4 load balancer", "L7 firewall").

OSI layer Name TCP/IP Examples Data unit
7 Application Application HTTP, DNS, SMTP, gRPC data/message
6 Presentation (in app) TLS, encoding, compression data
5 Session (in app) sessions, RPC setup data
4 Transport Transport TCP, UDP, QUIC segment/datagram
3 Network Internet IP, ICMP, routing packet
2 Data link Link Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP frame
1 Physical Link fibre, copper, radio bits

Decision gravity. Layering lets you swap one layer without touching others (HTTP over Wi-Fi or fibre, IPv4 or IPv6). The cost is some inefficiency and, as with QUIC, sometimes you break the layering on purpose to go faster. Layers are a two-way door in theory, but TCP and IP are effectively frozen because middleboxes (firewalls, NATs) assume them; this is called ossification, and it is why QUIC runs over UDP.

Industry examples. AWS NLB is L4 (fast, sees IP and port); AWS ALB is L7 (routes by URL and header). Nginx and Envoy do L7; HAProxy does both.

Everyday analogy. Sending a parcel: you write the letter (L7), a clerk packs and tracks it (L4), the sorting office reads the city (L3), the van driver only knows the next road (L2).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying TLS is "layer 6" as a fact. In real TCP/IP it is just a library above TCP; the OSI label is a convenience.
  • Saying a router works at L2. Routers are L3; switches are L2 (some are L3 capable).

notes.title: A host's first steps: before you type a URL
notes.html:
Before the browser can do anything, the machine must have network settings. On joining Wi-Fi, DHCP gives it: IP address (say 192.168.1.23), subnet mask (/24), default gateway (192.168.1.1) and DNS server (192.168.1.1 or 8.8.8.8). Details come in the next note.

You can see them:

# Linux
ip addr show wlan0          # IP and mask
ip route show               # default via 192.168.1.1
resolvectl status           # DNS servers
# Windows: ipconfig /all
$ ip route show
default via 192.168.1.1 dev wlan0 proto dhcp metric 600
192.168.1.0/24 dev wlan0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.23

Reading it: "to reach anything in 192.168.1.0/24 send directly; for everything else give the packet to 192.168.1.1."

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing the "default gateway" is the first hop for any off-subnet destination.
  • Forgetting that DNS server is a separate setting from the gateway.

notes.title: What happens when you type a URL: DNS
notes.html:
Step 1: turn www.example.com into an IP address. Browsers check caches first: browser cache, OS cache, then the configured resolver (often the ISP or 8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1).

If the resolver does not have it, it walks the tree: root server (.) says "ask the .com servers"; the .com TLD server says "ask example.com's nameserver"; that authoritative server returns the answer with a TTL.

$ dig www.example.com +noall +answer +stats
www.example.com.   3600  IN  A  93.184.216.34
;; Query time: 23 msec
;; SERVER: 1.1.1.1#53(1.1.1.1)

3600 is the TTL in seconds. +trace shows the whole walk from the root.

Worked example. Cold lookup: 4 round trips at ~20 ms each is ~80 ms; cached at the resolver: ~1 ms. A site with TTL 60 s is re-resolved every minute, which gives fast failover but more DNS load; TTL 86,400 is cheap but failover takes up to a day.

Industry examples. Route 53 and Cloudflare do latency and geo based answers (GeoDNS). Netflix and big CDNs use DNS to steer you to a nearby edge. The 2016 Dyn DDoS made Twitter, Reddit and GitHub vanish because they all used one DNS provider.

Decision gravity. Choosing a low TTL is easy to reverse, but only after the old long TTL expires, so lower it days before a migration. Using one DNS provider is a hidden single point of failure.

Everyday analogy. Looking up a friend's phone number: check your contacts (cache), ask a mutual friend (resolver), who may ask the phone book index (root, TLD, authoritative).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying DNS uses only UDP. It uses UDP 53 and falls back to TCP for large answers (and DNS over TLS/HTTPS exists).
  • Forgetting negative caching (NXDOMAIN is cached too).

notes.title: What happens when you type a URL: connecting
notes.html:
Step 2: open a TCP connection, then TLS, then send HTTP.

  1. ARP/routing: the destination IP is off-subnet, so the laptop sends the frame to the gateway's MAC (found by ARP).
  2. TCP 3-way handshake to port 443: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Costs 1 RTT.
  3. TLS 1.3 handshake: ClientHello with key share, ServerHello + certificate + Finished, client Finished. Costs 1 RTT (TLS 1.2 costs 2).
  4. HTTP request on the encrypted channel; the first response byte arrives after another RTT.

Worked example. Mumbai to a US-East server, RTT ~200 ms: DNS 200 ms (uncached) + TCP 200 + TLS 200 + request 200 = 800 ms before the first byte. With a CDN edge 10 ms away: 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 40 ms to the edge. HTTP/3 (QUIC) merges transport and TLS into 1 RTT, and 0 RTT on a resumed connection.

$ curl -so /dev/null -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} tcp:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n" https://example.com
dns:0.021 tcp:0.045 tls:0.098 ttfb:0.141 total:0.143

Industry examples. Google moved to QUIC to cut handshake time; Cloudflare and Fastly terminate TLS at the edge so the long-distance leg reuses a warm connection. Connection pooling in OkHttp (Android) exists precisely to avoid paying this 2 to 3 RTT cost per request.

Decision gravity. Connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing) is a pure win and reversible. Moving content to an edge is a cost decision with low lock-in.

Everyday analogy. Calling a company: dial and wait for pickup (TCP), agree on a secret language (TLS), only then ask your question (HTTP).

Common interview traps.

  • Counting only the HTTP round trip and ignoring DNS, TCP and TLS.
  • Not knowing that the TLS handshake is 1 RTT in 1.3 versus 2 in 1.2.

notes.title: What happens when you type a URL: the response and rendering
notes.html:
Step 3: the server answers, the browser renders. The load balancer picks a backend, which may call caches, databases and other services, then returns HTML with status 200 and headers (Cache-Control, Content-Type, Set-Cookie).

The browser parses HTML, finds more resources (CSS, JS, images), and fetches them, often in parallel over the same HTTP/2 connection. It builds the DOM and CSSOM, runs JS, lays out and paints.

$ curl -sI https://example.com
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
cache-control: max-age=604800
age: 331841
server: ECS (dcb/7F83)

age shows the CDN served a copy 331,841 s old: the origin was not even contacted.

Worked example. Page with 80 resources: HTTP/1.1 opens up to 6 connections per host, so 80 requests are about 14 waves. HTTP/2 sends all 80 on one connection concurrently, but one lost TCP packet stalls them all (head-of-line blocking at TCP), which HTTP/3 fixes.

Industry examples. Amazon found that every extra 100 ms of latency cost about 1% in sales (widely quoted, confirm exact figure before citing). Google uses Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) in search ranking.

Everyday analogy. Ordering at a restaurant: the waiter brings the menu (HTML), you notice you also need drinks, sides, dessert (more resources) and order them all together instead of one trip each.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing only the server side. A strong answer covers DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, server, rendering.
  • Forgetting caching layers: browser, CDN, reverse proxy, app, DB.

notes.title: Where a packet travels: hop by hop
notes.html:
A packet crosses 10 to 20 routers. Each router reads the destination IP, looks up the best next hop in its routing table, decrements TTL, and forwards. If TTL hits 0 the router drops it and sends back an ICMP "time exceeded"; traceroute abuses exactly this.

$ traceroute -n example.com
 1  192.168.1.1     1.2 ms     <- home router
 2  10.20.0.1       8.9 ms     <- ISP edge
 3  203.0.113.5    10.4 ms     <- ISP core
 4  198.51.100.9   24.8 ms     <- transit
 5  198.51.100.77  96.1 ms     <- undersea hop begins
 6  93.184.216.34  198 ms      <- destination

Worked example. Light in fibre travels ~200,000 km/s (2/3 of c). Mumbai to New York is ~12,500 km great circle, realistically ~15,000 km of cable: one way 75 ms, RTT 150 ms minimum. No engineering beats this physical floor.

Industry examples. Facebook's 6 October 2021 outage: a bad config withdrew its BGP routes and DNS servers, so no one could find Facebook's servers for about 6 hours. Packet-capture and traceroute were the debugging tools.

Everyday analogy. A relay race where each runner only knows the next runner's name, not the finish line.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the path is fixed. Each packet can take a different path; routes change.
  • Reading a * * * in traceroute as an outage; many routers just do not reply to ICMP.

notes.title: Debugging toolkit
notes.html:
Know the tool for each layer; interviewers love "the app is slow, what do you check?"

Layer Tool Question answered
L7/DNS dig, nslookup Does the name resolve and to what?
L7 curl -v -w Where does the time go?
L4 ss -tan, nc -vz host 443 Is the port open, what connection states?
L3 ping, traceroute, mtr Reachable, where is loss/latency?
L2 ip neigh, arp -a Which MAC for that IP?
All tcpdump, Wireshark What actually crossed the wire? 
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
mtr -rwc 20 example.com          # per-hop loss and latency report
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'tcp port 443 and host 93.184.216.34' -c 10
nc -vz example.com 443           # Connection to example.com 443 port [tcp/https] succeeded!
$ ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=117 time=18.4 ms
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=2 ttl=117 time=18.1 ms
--- 8.8.8.8 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 18.1/18.3/18.4/0.1 ms

Common interview traps.

  • Starting with the application logs when ping to the gateway would show a dead Wi-Fi in 2 seconds.
  • Concluding "ping works so the network is fine". ICMP can pass while TCP 443 is blocked.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• The internet is thousands of independent networks following shared protocols; delivery is best effort.
  • Data is encapsulated: app data, then TCP/UDP segment, IP packet, Ethernet frame. Frames live for one hop; packets for the whole path.
  • OSI has 7 layers, TCP/IP 4 or 5; know L2 (switch), L3 (router), L4 (TCP/UDP, NLB), L7 (HTTP, ALB).
  • URL flow: DNS, ARP to gateway, TCP handshake (1 RTT), TLS 1.3 (1 RTT), HTTP request, server work, render.
  • Latency has a physical floor (speed of light in fibre, about 5 ms per 1,000 km one way); fix it with caches, CDNs and connection reuse.
  • Debug bottom up: ping/mtr, dig, nc/ss, curl -w, tcpdump.

questions.promptHtml: Is the internet one network? Who runs it, and what happens when a link in the middle fails?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you see the internet as best-effort glued-together networks rather than a reliable "cloud".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The internet is about 100,000+ independent networks (autonomous systems: ISPs, clouds, companies) that agree to exchange traffic using shared protocols. Nobody owns it. It is best effort: packets can be lost, duplicated or reordered, and routers find another path when a link dies. Reliability is built at the edges, mostly by TCP.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each autonomous system runs its own internal network and announces to its neighbours which IP ranges it can reach. Those announcements (BGP) are the glue. A packet crosses several of these networks, each making a local forwarding decision.

Phone -> Wi-Fi router -> ISP -> Transit backbone -> Cloud provider -> Server
          (home)        (AS A)    (AS B)             (AS C)

When a link fails, routers withdraw the routes through it and traffic shifts to alternates. Packets in flight on the dead link are simply lost; TCP retransmits them. About 95% of intercontinental traffic rides undersea fibre, so "the cloud" is cables and routers.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the network guarantees delivery. It does not; endpoints do.
  • Thinking one company controls routing.
  • Ignoring physical reality (cable cuts do happen).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is an autonomous system? -> An independently administered network with its own AS number that speaks BGP to peers.
  2. Who guarantees delivery then? -> TCP at the endpoints, or the application for UDP.
  3. How long does re-routing take after a cut? -> IGP in seconds to sub-second, BGP convergence can take tens of seconds to minutes; verify per provider.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "a global network of computers". Senior: independent ASes, best-effort delivery, edge-based reliability, and that failure handling is the design assumption, so apps need retries and timeouts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that assume the network is reliable skip timeouts and retries, then hang when one transit link drops packets.

questions.promptHtml: What is encapsulation? Name the unit of data at each layer and which address each layer uses.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundation for every debugging question: which header is which, and which address changes per hop.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each layer wraps the data from above with its own header. The app writes bytes, TCP adds ports (segment), IP adds source and destination IP (packet), and Ethernet or Wi-Fi adds MAC addresses (frame) for one link only. IP addresses stay the same end to end; MAC addresses are rewritten at every hop.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HTTP bytes
[TCP hdr 20B | data]                    segment  (ports)
[IP hdr 20B  | TCP seg]                 packet   (IPs)
[Eth 14B | IP packet | FCS 4B]          frame    (MACs)

With a 1500-byte MTU: 1500 - 20 (IP) - 20 (TCP) = 1460 bytes payload (MSS). A 2 MB page is roughly 1,440 packets. A router strips the frame, reads the IP header, picks the next hop, then builds a new frame with new MACs and a decremented TTL.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying MAC addresses travel end to end.
  • Mixing up "packet" and "frame".
  • Forgetting header overhead when computing throughput.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What changes at a router? -> MACs, TTL, IP checksum; src/dst IP stay unless NAT.
  2. What is MSS vs MTU? -> MTU is the link's max IP packet; MSS is the max TCP payload (MTU minus headers).
  3. What if the packet exceeds the MTU? -> Fragment (IPv4, DF=0) or drop and send ICMP "frag needed" when DF=1.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the layers. Senior ties it to MTU, MSS and why VPN or VXLAN overhead causes mysterious stalls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Overlay networks add 50 bytes (VXLAN) and a mis-set MTU silently drops large packets while pings work.

questions.promptHtml: Explain OSI vs TCP/IP models. Where do a switch, a router, TLS and an "L7 load balancer" sit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Layer vocabulary is how engineers localise faults and pick infrastructure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: OSI has 7 layers, TCP/IP collapses it to 4 (link, internet, transport, application). A switch works at L2 on MACs, a router at L3 on IPs, TCP/UDP is L4 on ports, and an L7 load balancer reads HTTP. TLS has no clean slot; it sits around L5-L6 above TCP.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
OSI TCP/IP Example
7 App, 6 Pres, 5 Session Application HTTP, DNS, TLS
4 Transport Transport TCP, UDP, QUIC (over UDP)
3 Network Internet IP, ICMP, BGP routes
2 Data link, 1 Physical Link Ethernet, Wi-Fi

An L4 LB picks a backend using IP and port only (cheap, can't see URLs, preserves TLS end to end if passthrough). An L7 LB terminates TLS, parses HTTP and routes by host or path, at higher CPU cost.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Insisting TLS is exactly L6.
  • Calling everything "layer 7".
  • Believing OSI is what the internet runs; TCP/IP is.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which layer does ping use? -> ICMP, riding on IP (L3).
  2. Is QUIC L4? -> It provides L4-like services in user space over UDP.
  3. Why choose L4 over L7 LB? -> Throughput, latency, non-HTTP protocols; lose content routing and HTTP metrics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites names. Senior uses layers to pick tools: tcpdump for L2-L4, curl -v for L7, and explains cost trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team put an L4 NLB in front and then wondered why path-based routing didn't work.

questions.contextHtml:
Monday 9:05. 40 laptops on the new 4th-floor Wi-Fi can open nothing. Floors 1-3 are fine. A laptop shows:

$ ip addr show wlan0
inet 169.254.37.12/16 scope link
$ ip route
169.254.0.0/16 dev wlan0 scope link

The Wi-Fi shows connected with full signal. The network team says the DHCP server's CPU is 5% and "nothing changed". A new switch was installed on Friday for floor 4.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what is happening and how you fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the Wi-Fi or reboot the laptops." Ignores the 169.254 address, which is the key clue, and never asks where DHCP discovery goes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is floor 4 on its own VLAN or subnet? Is there a DHCP relay (ip helper-address) configured for that VLAN? Do wired devices on floor 4 also fail? Did anyone change a DHCP scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Give floor 4 a static range or temporarily bridge the AP uplink to a VLAN that already has DHCP relay, so people can work.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) New VLAN has no relay, so broadcasts never reach the server. (b) Trunk allows the wrong VLANs. (c) Scope for the new subnet missing or exhausted. (d) Rogue or blocked DHCP (snooping). Red herring: server CPU is irrelevant if requests never arrive.
  4. How I'd verify each: On the DHCP server tcpdump -ni eth0 port 67 or port 68 and watch for Discovers from floor 4. On a laptop capture:
00:00:01 IP 0.0.0.0.68 > 255.255.255.255.67: BOOTP/DHCP, Request, DHCP: Discover
00:00:04 IP 0.0.0.0.68 > 255.255.255.255.67: BOOTP/DHCP, Request, DHCP: Discover
(no Offer)

Check the switch show vlan, trunk allowed list and relay config. 5. Root cause: DHCP Discover is a broadcast (255.255.255.255) that dies at the router. Without a relay on the new VLAN's gateway interface, the server never sees it, so the OS self-assigns a link-local 169.254.x.x (APIPA) address. 6. Fix: Short term: add ip helper-address <dhcp-server> on the VLAN interface and create a scope for the new subnet. Long term: template the VLAN provisioning so relay and scope are created together. 7. Prevention: Alert on a spike of 169.254 clients, a provisioning checklist, DHCP scope-utilisation monitoring. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a second DHCP server on the floor (rogue-server risk), and not widen the scope blindly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Relay works but clients still fail? -> Check DHCP snooping trusted ports and scope exhaustion.
  • Clients get an IP but cannot reach the internet? -> Check the default gateway option and DNS option in the lease.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A new office wing went live with everything correct except the relay line; the fix was one command, but the diagnosis took two hours because everyone checked the server first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reboots devices, ignores 169.254.
  • Hire: identifies DHCP broadcast not reaching the server and checks the relay.
  • Strong hire: captures on both sides, explains why broadcast does not cross routers, and adds provisioning guardrails.

questions.subtopic: What happens when you type a URL
questions.promptHtml: After DNS returns an IP, how many round trips before the first byte of an HTTPS page arrives? How do you cut it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can count RTTs and know why latency, not bandwidth, dominates small requests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TCP handshake is 1 RTT, TLS 1.3 adds 1 more, then the HTTP request/response is another, so about 3 RTT after DNS. TLS 1.2 adds one more. You cut it with connection reuse, TLS 1.3 session resumption/0-RTT, HTTP/2 multiplexing, QUIC (which merges transport and crypto handshakes), and CDNs that shorten the RTT.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client                      Server
 SYN  ------------------->          \
      <------------------ SYN-ACK    } 1 RTT (TCP)
 ACK + ClientHello ------>          /
      <------ ServerHello, cert, Finished   } 1 RTT (TLS 1.3)
 Finished + GET / -------->
      <------------------ 200 + data        } 1 RTT (HTTP)

At 100 ms RTT that is 300 ms before the first byte, regardless of bandwidth. A keep-alive connection pays zero of the first two. 0-RTT resumption sends data in the first flight but is replayable, so only for idempotent requests.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting DNS as an extra RTT.
  • Claiming bandwidth upgrades fix this.
  • Using 0-RTT for POSTs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 cost? -> 2 RTT vs 1 RTT for the handshake.
  2. Why does QUIC help? -> One combined handshake, no TCP head-of-line blocking across streams.
  3. Risk of 0-RTT? -> Replay attacks; limit to safe methods.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "three-way handshake then request". Senior counts RTTs, quantifies at a given RTT, and lists concrete mitigations including edge termination.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving TLS termination to a CDN edge 10 ms away turned a 300 ms first byte into about 130 ms without touching the origin.

questions.contextHtml:
Users report the checkout page "sometimes takes 5+ seconds". The app team says p99 server time is 120 ms. You run curl from a bastion in the same region:

$ curl -o /dev/null -s -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} connect:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n" https://shop.example.com/checkout
dns:2.003 connect:2.021 tls:2.058 ttfb:2.190 total:2.251

Another run returns dns:0.004. The resolver is a pair of VMs at 10.0.0.2 and 10.0.0.3. The CPU on the web tier is 20%.
questions.promptHtml: What do you conclude and what do you do next?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale the web servers or add caching." The server is 130 ms; the extra time is before the connection exists.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the delay always about 2 s or 5 s multiples? Does /etc/resolv.conf list both resolvers? Does it hit all clients or one AZ?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the failing resolver from DHCP/resolv.conf or fix it; set options timeout:1 attempts:2 rotate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One resolver is dead or dropping, and the stub tries it first with a timeout. UDP loss on the DNS path. Resolver cache cold or overloaded. Red herring: the app and TLS (58 ms).
  4. How I'd verify each: dig @10.0.0.2 shop.example.com and dig @10.0.0.3 ... with +time=1 +tries=1; tcpdump -ni any port 53 to see queries with no reply; check resolver logs and conntrack drops.
  5. Root cause: The glibc resolver waits 5 s by default per attempt per server; the 2.0 s here means one query was lost and retried. Every first lookup after the TTL expiry that hits the sick resolver pays the timeout.
  6. Fix: Repair or replace the bad resolver; configure retry timeouts; add a node-local DNS cache.
  7. Prevention: Synthetic probe that times DNS separately, alert on resolver packet loss and latency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise TTLs as a band-aid (hurts failover), not blame the CDN.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why do repeat requests look fine? -> The answer is cached locally or in a healthy resolver until TTL expiry.
  • Only containers affected? -> Check the container's resolv.conf ndots and search domains causing multiple lookups.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "application slowness" ticket survived three sprints before someone split timings with curl -w and found one resolver silently dropping 30% of queries.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the app.
  • Hire: reads the timing breakdown and isolates DNS.
  • Strong hire: proves the dead resolver with captures and fixes client timeouts plus monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
A customer says your API is slow from Frankfurt. They send a traceroute:

 1  192.168.1.1     1.1 ms
 2  10.20.0.1       3.4 ms
 3  * * *
 4  be5.core1.fra   9.8 ms
 5  ae7.edge2.ams   212.5 ms
 6  72.14.200.9     15.2 ms
 7  api.example.com 16.0 ms

Your on-call says "hop 5 is 212 ms, the problem is at the AMS router, call the carrier."

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts hop 5 as the culprit. Ignores that hop 6 and the destination are fast, so end-to-end is 16 ms.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the actual API latency look like (curl timing)? Is loss present in the final hop? Is it the forward or return path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed yet; first confirm there is a real problem at the destination.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Router deprioritises ICMP TTL-exceeded generation (control plane rate limit), so that hop looks slow while forwarding is fine. Hop 3 * * * is a firewall blocking ICMP. Return path asymmetry. A real problem elsewhere (app, TLS).
  4. How I'd verify each: mtr -rwzbc 100 api.example.com to see loss and latency per hop over time; judge only if loss or latency persists to later hops. Use curl -w timings and a TCP traceroute (traceroute -T -p 443).
  5. Root cause: traceroute measures the time for each router to generate an ICMP reply, which is a slow-path control-plane task. Transit traffic is forwarded in hardware, so hop 5 latency does not propagate to hop 6 and 7. The path is healthy.
  6. Fix: Respond with data: path total is 16 ms. If the customer still sees slowness, investigate DNS, TLS and app time.
  7. Prevention: Provide an mtr/curl runbook to support and teach the "later hops fine means ignore" rule.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not open a carrier ticket on one hop; not treat * as packet loss.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Latency rises at hop 5 and stays high to the end? -> Then real congestion or a long path; check the reverse path.
  • Why can the return path differ? -> Routing is per direction (hot-potato), so asymmetric is normal.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A customer escalated "212 ms at our peer" for a week; a TCP-based mtr showed the router was just rate limiting ICMP.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames hop 5.
  • Hire: recognises ICMP deprioritisation and reads the end-to-end figure.
  • Strong hire: uses mtr/TCP probes, discusses asymmetry and gives the customer a clear explanation.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through how www.example.com gets resolved, including caches and who talks to whom.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: DNS is the first dependency of every request; failure modes here look like "the app is down".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The browser checks its cache, then the OS stub resolver (hosts file, local cache), then sends a recursive query to the configured resolver (ISP or 8.8.8.8). On a miss, that resolver iterates: root servers point to the .com TLD servers, which point to example.com's authoritative servers, which answer with the A/AAAA record and a TTL. Every layer caches until TTL expires.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Browser -> OS stub -> Recursive resolver -> Root (.)       "ask .com"
                                         -> TLD (.com)     "ask ns1.example.com"
                                         -> Authoritative  "A 93.184.216.34 TTL 300"

Uses UDP port 53 for small answers; falls back to TCP for large responses or zone transfers (and DoT/DoH encrypt it). Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too. Results of CNAME chains add lookups. A cold lookup is 1-4 RTTs to different servers; a warm one is under 1 ms.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
dig +trace www.example.com
dig www.example.com +noall +answer   # shows remaining TTL

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the client talks to root servers directly.
  • Lowering TTL after a migration (it only affects future caches).
  • Ignoring negative caching.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Recursive vs authoritative? -> Recursive does the legwork and caches; authoritative owns the zone data.
  2. CNAME at the apex? -> Not allowed in standard DNS; use ALIAS/ANAME at the provider.
  3. Why do some resolvers ignore TTL? -> Min-TTL clamping, buggy caches, and JVM networkaddress.cache.ttl.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the hierarchy. Senior adds caching layers, TTL planning, UDP vs TCP, and the JVM/OS caching surprises.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A JVM caching DNS forever kept sending traffic to a decommissioned load balancer IP.

questions.contextHtml:
After enabling a site-to-site IPsec tunnel between a DC and AWS, small API calls work and ping works, but file uploads over ~1.4 KB hang. Capture on the client:

10:01:02.100 IP 10.1.0.5.51234 > 172.16.4.9.443: Flags [S],  mss 1460
10:01:02.140 IP 172.16.4.9.443 > 10.1.0.5.51234: Flags [S.], mss 1460
10:01:02.141 IP 10.1.0.5.51234 > 172.16.4.9.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:1461, length 1460
10:01:03.141 IP 10.1.0.5.51234 > 172.16.4.9.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:1461, length 1460  (retransmit)
10:01:05.141 IP ... retransmit

The tunnel adds about 73 bytes of overhead; interface MTU is 1500 everywhere. Firewalls block all ICMP "for security".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network is flaky, open a ticket." Misses that handshake and tiny packets succeed while full-size ones die.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is DF set? What is the tunnel's effective MTU? Are ICMP type 3 code 4 messages being dropped anywhere? Does it fail in one direction only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Clamp MSS on the tunnel interface (iptables -t mangle ... --clamp-mss-to-pmtu) or lower the interface MTU to 1400.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: PMTU black hole (1500-byte packets plus 73 bytes exceeds path MTU, ICMP frag-needed blocked). Asymmetric route. Firewall dropping fragments. Red herring: handshake succeeded so "it's not a firewall".
  4. How I'd verify each: ping -M do -s 1372 172.16.4.9 and step the size up to find the max; tracepath 172.16.4.9 shows pmtu; capture for ICMP type 3 code 4 on both ends.
  5. Root cause: The sender uses DF=1 and 1500-byte packets, which after encapsulation need 1573 bytes. The router should return ICMP "fragmentation needed", but ICMP is blocked, so the sender never learns and keeps retransmitting the same size. SYN packets are tiny, so the handshake works.
  6. Fix: Short term: MSS clamp to about 1360 on the tunnel. Long term: allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (and ICMPv6 Packet Too Big) through firewalls; set consistent MTUs; enable tcp_mtu_probing=1.
  7. Prevention: Test with large pings after any tunnel or overlay change; document overhead budgets per encapsulation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not clear DF globally (fragmentation hurts performance and middleboxes drop fragments); do not blanket-block ICMP.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• UDP-based apps (DNS, QUIC) still fail? -> MSS clamp only fixes TCP; fix MTU or application packet size.
  • IPv6? -> Routers never fragment, so ICMPv6 PTB is mandatory.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A VPN migration passed every smoke test with curl and ping and died on the first S3 multi-part upload; the only clue was retransmits of identical lengths.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts tunnels.
  • Hire: identifies MTU and ICMP blocking, applies MSS clamp.
  • Strong hire: computes overhead, finds the exact PMTU, explains DF and UDP/IPv6 implications.

questions.contextHtml: You must move api.example.com from a load balancer in region A (A record 203.0.113.10, TTL 86400) to region B (198.51.100.20) with no more than 0.1% failed requests. Traffic is 8k req/s. Mobile apps and some partners are known to ignore TTLs. Cutover window is next Saturday; today is Monday.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Change the record on Saturday and lower the TTL then." The old 24h TTL is already cached everywhere.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can both regions serve the same data (replication)? Do clients pin IPs? Is a health-check-based or weighted DNS feature available? Are there allowlists on partner firewalls?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Today, lower the TTL to 60 s. Caches that hold the old 86400 value expire at most 24 h later, so wait at least 24-48 h before cutover.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: stale caches beyond TTL, partners with IP allowlists, state divergence, TLS cert on the new LB, clients with hard-coded IPs.
  4. How I'd verify each: dig against several public resolvers for remaining TTL; log source IPs hitting the old LB over time to measure the long tail; test new region with a canary hostname and curl --resolve.
  5. Root cause: DNS changes propagate by cache expiry, not by push. TTL decides the stale window, and the TTL you set now only takes effect once old entries expire.
  6. Fix/plan: Monday: TTL to 60. Wed: weighted records 1% to B, then 10%, 50%, 100%, watching error rates. Keep region A serving (or proxy to B) for at least 48 h after 100%, because stragglers will keep arriving. Raise TTL back afterwards.
  7. Prevention: Keep TTLs moderate (300 s) for critical records; avoid IP allowlists by offering stable anycast or published ranges.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on a hard flip; not decommission A until the access log shows near-zero traffic. Low TTL raises resolver load and lookup latency slightly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Partner allowlist the old IP? -> Coordinate their change first; keep A forwarding to B.
  • Region B fails mid-cutover? -> Weighted/health-checked records and a rollback by setting weights back (effective after TTL).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cutover looked clean at 99.9% and the remaining 0.1% were IoT devices holding the old IP for weeks; the old LB had to stay up as a forwarder.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips the record.
  • Hire: pre-lowers TTL and stages traffic.
  • Strong hire: measures the long tail, keeps the old side alive, plans rollback and partner coordination.

questions.contextHtml:
A static marketing page takes 3.4 s to render for users in Singapore; origin is in us-east (RTT ~230 ms). The page is 1 HTML file that references 6 CSS/JS files on the same host and 2 on another host. A HAR summary:

html      connect 232ms  tls 465ms  ttfb 240ms   (total 940ms)
app.js    connect 0      tls 0      ttfb 245ms
style.css connect 0      ttfb 244ms
fonts.x.com connect 230ms tls 460ms ttfb 235ms
hero.jpg (2.1 MB) download 1.9 s

HTTP/1.1, TLS 1.2. No CDN. The team proposes "bigger origin servers".
questions.promptHtml: Where does the time go and what do you change, in order of payoff?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Scale the origin; origin processing is only a few ms of the TTFB.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can static assets go through a CDN? Is HTTP/2 or 3 available? Is the hero image optimisable? Is the second host critical (fonts)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a CDN in front with an edge in Singapore and cache HTML/static assets.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: RTT-bound handshakes (connect 232 + TLS 465 = ~700 ms before the first request). Extra connections to a third-party host repeat that cost. Large image on a long-RTT path. Serial request waterfall. Red herring: server CPU.
  4. How I'd verify each: Browser devtools waterfall, curl -w timings from a Singapore probe, WebPageTest from that region; compare after CDN with the same probe.
  5. Root cause: Round trips, not compute. TLS 1.2 costs 2 RTT after TCP's 1; each new host repeats it; the image is 2.1 MB over slow-start congestion windows at 230 ms RTT, taking many RTTs.
  6. Fix: CDN edge terminates TCP/TLS 10-20 ms away (handshakes drop to ~60 ms), TLS 1.3, HTTP/2 or 3, self-host fonts, compress images (WebP/AVIF, 200 KB), preconnect hints, long cache headers.
  7. Prevention: Real-user monitoring by region and a performance budget in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not spend on bigger origin; CDN adds cache invalidation and cost; HTTP/3 may be blocked on some networks, so keep fallback.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Dynamic API calls still slow? -> The edge cannot cache them; use persistent origin connections from edge, or regional deployments.
  • Why not just compress HTML more? -> It is not the bottleneck.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch page dropped from 4 s to 0.9 s in Asia by just adding a CDN and removing one third-party font host, with zero origin change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales servers.
  • Hire: spots handshake RTT cost and CDN.
  • Strong hire: quantifies RTT budget, orders fixes by payoff, and covers dynamic content limits.

questions.promptHtml: How does traceroute work, why can it lie, and how does TTL protect the network?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests deep understanding of hop-by-hop forwarding and diagnostic tools' limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every router decrements the IP TTL (hop limit); at zero it drops the packet and returns ICMP Time Exceeded. Traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3, and so on, and records who replies at each step. It lies because replies are control-plane traffic that may be rate limited or blocked, paths are per-direction and per-flow (ECMP), and probes may take a different path from your real traffic.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
TTL=1 -> R1 replies Time Exceeded
TTL=2 -> R2 replies ...
TTL=N -> destination replies Port Unreachable (UDP probe) or Echo Reply (ICMP probe)

TTL stops forwarding loops from circulating forever (typical start 64 or 128). ECMP hashes the 5-tuple, so probes with changing UDP ports may traverse different parallel paths, showing a Frankenstein route. The listed hop is the ingress interface of the replying router, and the reverse path can differ entirely, so a latency number includes the unseen return trip.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
traceroute -T -p 443 api.example.com   # TCP probes pass firewalls that block UDP/ICMP
mtr -rwzc 100 api.example.com

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Judging a hop by its RTT alone.
  • Treating * * * as an outage.
  • Forgetting MPLS tunnels hide hops.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why use TCP traceroute? -> It follows the same filters and ECMP hash as real traffic.
  2. Paris traceroute? -> Keeps the flow identifier constant so ECMP paths stay consistent.
  3. How do you find the reverse path? -> Run from the other end or use a looking glass.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it shows the hops". Senior knows the TTL mechanism, ICMP rate limiting, ECMP and asymmetry, and picks TCP-based tools.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A partner outage was "found" at a router that was merely rate limiting ICMP while traffic flowed fine.

questions.contextHtml:
You run a gRPC (HTTP/2) microservice fleet: 300 pods, 60k req/s, long-lived connections from 40 client services. After adding a classic L4 load balancer, you notice one backend pod gets 38% of the traffic while 20 pods are idle. CPU graph:

pod-a  92%   pod-b  88%   pod-c  4%   pod-d  3%   ... (most pods < 5%)

The LB distributes connections round-robin evenly. Product wants zero-downtime deploys and per-route canaries.
questions.promptHtml: Why is balancing skewed and which layer should balance this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to least-connections." Doesn't understand HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one long-lived connection.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many connections per client? Do clients use client-side LB? What are the request size and duration distributions? Is mTLS required end to end?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make clients reconnect periodically (max connection age / GOAWAY) to spread load, and scale hot pods.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: L4 balances connections, not requests; HTTP/2 pins thousands of requests to one connection. A few heavy clients each hold one connection. Uneven request cost. Red herring: LB algorithm choice.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-pod request counters, ss -tn state established '( sport = :8080 )' | wc -l per pod, and per-client connection counts.
  5. Root cause: Layer mismatch. The L4 LB sees connections (L4); gRPC's unit of work is a stream (L7). Even connection distribution still yields skewed request distribution.
  6. Fix: Short term: max-connection-age 30 s with GOAWAY. Long term: L7 proxy (Envoy/service mesh) or gRPC client-side load balancing with a headless service, giving per-request balancing, retries and canary routing.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards on per-backend request rate skew; load-test with realistic long-lived connections.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: L7 costs CPU and an extra hop of latency (sub-ms to 1 ms) plus TLS termination handling; not go back to round robin L4 for HTTP/2.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Needs end-to-end mTLS? -> Mesh sidecars with mTLS between proxies, or L7 passthrough with SNI-only routing losing path routing.
  • Client-side LB downsides? -> Every client needs discovery and logic; harder across languages.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "balanced" fleet had two pods at 90% CPU for weeks because each of the heaviest clients held a single persistent connection.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries different L4 algorithms.
  • Hire: explains connection vs request and moves to L7 or client-side LB.
  • Strong hire: includes GOAWAY mitigation, trade-offs, and canary and mTLS implications.

questions.contextHtml: A VP says "the app feels slow for our customers in Brazil, make the network faster". You have no more details. The service is hosted in us-east-1. Support tickets come from three Brazilian ISPs. Real-user monitoring shows p50 TTFB 620 ms in Brazil vs 180 ms in the US. Budget: moderate.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this into an actionable plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy a bigger link" or "add a CDN" without measuring. Treats the network as one unknown.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the target (p50 or p95, which pages)? Which flows matter (login, API, static)? Are there data residency rules? Is the slowness on all ISPs equally?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable CDN caching for static content and compression; quick win, low risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Pure distance and handshake RTTs (about 120-140 ms RTT, 3 RTT before first byte is ~400 ms). Poor peering of specific ISPs, taking a detour via Miami or Europe. Uncached dynamic calls. Packet loss on last mile.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-ISP RUM breakdown (DNS, connect, TLS, TTFB); traceroute and mtr from probes inside each ISP; compare to a CDN-fronted test; check loss with mtr.
  5. Root cause: Typically a mix: physics (~65 ms one way minimum from SP to Virginia), multiple handshake round trips, and one or two ISPs with indirect routes.
  6. Fix: Edge termination (CDN or accelerator) in Sao Paulo, TLS 1.3 + HTTP/2/3, connection reuse to origin, cache API responses where safe; if still above target, deploy a read replica region in sa-east-1.
  7. Prevention: SLOs by region and ISP, synthetic probes from key markets.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Multi-region data costs consistency and money, so only after edge termination proves insufficient. Do not promise a number before measurement.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One ISP is 3x worse than the others? -> Peering or routing issue; try a CDN with better interconnect or work with the ISP.
  • Writes must stay in the US? -> Keep writes central, push edge reads, and make the client optimistic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "network is slow" ticket became a two-line fix once per-ISP RUM showed one carrier routing via another continent.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: guesses solutions.
  • Hire: asks for target and measures RTT components.
  • Strong hire: separates physics from fixable issues, stages cost-ordered fixes with measurable goals.
